t: 3235. Check if the Rectangle Corner Is Reachable
o: Circles act as obstacles; a valid path must stay strictly inside the rectangle and avoid all circles. The path is blocked exactly when some set of mutually-connected circles (connected via intersection points lying inside the rectangle) forms a barrier attached to the rectangle boundary. Geometrically, any connected chain of circles touching two distinct sides of the rectangle seals off at least one corner (opposite sides split the rectangle; adjacent sides trap their shared corner together with the boundary arc). So: union-find circles whose boundaries intersect inside the rectangle; then false iff some component touches ≥ 2 distinct edges. Example 2's circle touches left and top → false; example 3's two circles intersect and touch right and top → false; examples 1 and 4 touch at most one edge → true.
k: Barrier criterion: a component of intersecting circles touching two distinct rectangle edges blocks a corner.
Circle–circle connections count only if an intersection point lies inside the rectangle.
Distance-from-center-to-segment tests edge contact; clamp the projection onto the segment.

a.i: Model circles as nodes. Union pairs whose boundaries intersect at a point inside the rectangle (compute both intersection points of the boundary circles and test them). For each circle test contact with each of the four edges via point-to-segment distance ≤ r. If any union-find component records contacts with two different edges, no path exists.
s: For each pair, if boundary circles intersect and an intersection point is in the rectangle, union them.
For each circle, mark edge contacts L/R/T/B using segment-distance ≤ r.
Return false iff some root has two distinct edge marks; else true.
a.t: O(n² α(n)) for n ≤ 1000 circles — all pairs checked once
a.sp: O(n) for the DSU and edge marks

w: The heart of this problem is the geometric reduction — once you see 'connected circles touching two edges block', the DSU is boilerplate. Pitfalls: forgetting to require intersection points inside the rectangle (circles may link outside the rectangle without blocking anything), using center distance instead of segment distance for edge contact, and precision issues with coordinates up to 10⁹ (use doubles/long doubles; exact rational checks are safer if needed). Follow-up: report an actual witness path, or handle obstacles shaped as rectangles.
